solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Staggered idiot screwed up a debut

parts.note: a tit is British slang for a fool

indicators.note: Something screwed up is crumpled out of shape, so the letters lose their order.

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A nervous performer tottered through a first night they had botched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Idiot screwed up a debut' reads as one story of a fool fluffing a first appearance; only 'a debut' is jumbled, and the fool comes first as a short slang word.
explanation.definitionFit: To titubate is a rare, learned verb for to stagger or totter, so the past tenses match.

clue.text: Extremely tasty rum goes into hot alcoholic drink

indicators.note: The rum word goes into the gap between the two outer letters.
The extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its first and last letters are kept.

parts.note: the outer letters of TastY
rum is British for strange or odd

explanation.surface: A tasty dash of rum poured into a hot drink.
explanation.walkthrough: With a hot drink in view, 'rum' is surely the spirit; it is the old British adjective, as in 'a rum business'.
explanation.definitionFit: A toddy is spirits, usually whisky, mixed with hot water, sugar and spices.

clue.text: Defeat obsession about series of bad events

indicators.note: 'About' means around, so the obsession word goes round the other.

parts.note: to have a thing about something is to be obsessed with it
a rash of burglaries is a spate of them

explanation.surface: Someone crushed by their fixation on a run of misfortune.
explanation.walkthrough: A rash in this sense is a sudden outbreak of unwelcome happenings, as with a rash of complaints.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrashing is a heavy defeat, so the nouns match.

clue.text: Living religious academic stops cohabiting

indicators.note: Something that stops a gap plugs it, so the academic sits inside the living word.

parts.note: being = existing, living
DD is a Doctor of Divinity

explanation.surface: A devout scholar living in sin gives it up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stops' looks like the verb of giving something up, which completes the moral tale; it is the plug that fills a hole.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedding someone is sleeping with them, which a loose reading of cohabiting covers.

clue.text: Chap interrupts fool in meal for some water

indicators.note: Something that interrupts breaks in, so the chap sits in the middle of the fool word.

parts.note: tea is the British early-evening meal

indicators.note: 'In' puts that combination inside the meal word.

parts.note: an ass is a fool
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: A man butts in on a fool at dinner to ask for a glass of water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some water' sounds like a drink at the table; it is a whole sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tasman Sea lies between Australia and New Zealand, a body of water.

clue.text: Doctor swallowing peeled potato chips gets more thirsty

indicators.note: Peeling takes off the skin, so the outer letters go.
The doctor's letters swallow the others, taking them inside.

parts.note: Dr = doctor
FRIES, potato chips, without the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A doctor wolfing down salty chips ends up wanting a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potato chips' here is the American name for fries, the long strips British people call chips.
explanation.definitionFit: Drier means more dry, and dry is a common word for thirsty.

clue.text: Keen music half-heartedly backed

indicators.note: The heart of a word is its middle, here the double G, and only half of it stays.
Backed means sent backwards, so the letters run from the end.

parts.note: REGGAE, Jamaican music, with one of its two middle Gs gone

explanation.surface: Someone keen on music who backs it only half-heartedly.
explanation.walkthrough: The heart of REGGAE is the GG at its centre, so losing half the heart removes a single G.
explanation.definitionFit: Keen and eager are plain synonyms for enthusiastic.

clue.text: Newly formed Linear C not in need of deciphering

indicators.note: The letters are formed anew into a different arrangement.

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A newly discovered ancient script, Linear C, that turns out to need no decipherment.
explanation.walkthrough: Linear A and Linear B are ancient Cretan scripts, and B was famously deciphered; there is no Linear C, so the name is a hint.
explanation.definitionFit: En clair is French for 'in clear', used of messages sent in plain language, not code.

clue.text: Spirit served by good landlord

parts.note: g = good
a pub landlord is mine host

explanation.surface: A spirit poured by a decent pub landlord.
explanation.walkthrough: With a landlord behind the bar, 'Spirit' is a measure of whisky; it is a phantom. A British landlord is the keeper of a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A ghost is the spirit of a dead person, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Mention concerning engineers crushed by barrier

parts.note: re = concerning, as in a letter heading

indicators.note: Something crushed by another is pressed in on all sides by it.

parts.note: a fence is a barrier
RE = Royal Engineers, the British army corps

explanation.surface: A report about engineers pinned under a collapsed barrier.
explanation.walkthrough: The same two letters come twice from different words: RE for 'concerning', then RE for the Royal Engineers inside the barrier.
explanation.definitionFit: A mention of something is a reference to it; both are nouns (or verbs).

clue.text: Challenged boxer, ultimately in late round

indicators.note: Letters sent round are turned about and come out in a new order.
Ultimately means at the end, so the last letter is taken.

parts.note: the last letter of boxeR
the late king is the dead king

explanation.surface: A boxer who was challenged and went down in the last round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late round' reads as a final round of a fight; 'late' means deceased and 'round' stirs the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To dare someone is to challenge them, so dared matches challenged in tense.

clue.text: Rod disinclined to cease paying attention

parts.note: a switch is a thin flexible rod or cane
to be off something is to have lost the taste for it

explanation.surface: Rod is reluctant to stop listening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rod' looks like a man's name; it is a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: To switch off is to stop paying attention, as a bored listener does.

clue.text: Faith school is heavy going

indicators.note: Letters on the go move about and settle in a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Life at a religious school is hard work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavy going' is one idiom for hard work; it splits, with 'heavy' joining the fodder and 'going' as the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A yeshiva is an Orthodox Jewish college for study of the Talmud, a school of faith.

clue.text: Scorching day — daughter abandons open American car

indicators.note: The daughter abandons the car, so her letter leaves it.

parts.note: a roadster is an open two-seater car, a chiefly American name
d = daughter

explanation.surface: On a blistering day a daughter leaves her open-topped car.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'Scorching day' look like the setting for the story; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A roaster is an informal word for a very hot day.

clue.text: Twist with band

parts.note: w = with
a ring is a band, as round a finger

explanation.walkthrough: 'Twist' could be a dance or a band's hit; it is the definition, and 'with' shrinks to one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To wring something is to twist it, as when wringing out a cloth.

clue.text: Watering hole bar keeps limitless milk stout

indicators.note: Without limits the word loses both its ends.

parts.note: a well is a hole dug for water

indicators.note: The bar word keeps the milk letters inside it.

parts.note: bar and but both mean except
MILK without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A pub that stocks milk stout with no limit on supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watering hole' and 'bar' both look like pubs and 'milk stout' like a beer; the first is a well, the second means except.
explanation.definitionFit: Stout describes a person of heavy, sturdy build, which is what well-built means.

clue.text: One could have steamers turning north

definitions.text: One could have steamers turning north

indicators.note: Turning the letters over puts them in a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder
n = north

explanation.surface: Someone at the helm swinging ships round to head north.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: a steersman is exactly the one who turns steamers to a new heading.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the whole clue describes the person at the helm, whose job is to bring a ship's head round to a new bearing.

clue.text: X-ray celeb in a bad way — in a very bad way

indicators.note: Letters in a bad way are in a mess, out of their proper order.

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A celebrity's X-ray shows they are in a very bad way.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue repeats 'in a bad way' so that the first is the instruction and the second, intensified, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverb for an adverbial phrase: execrable is a strong word for dreadful, so the clue adds 'very' to match its force.

clue.text: Beggar's correct trick cycling

indicators.note: Cycling moves letters round from one end to the other, here the A from the front to the back.

parts.note: to mend a fault is to correct it
an antic is a prank or trick

explanation.surface: A beggar pulls a cycling stunt to earn coins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beggar’s' reads as possessive; the 's stands for 'is'. Cycled once, ANTIC becomes ICANT.
explanation.definitionFit: A mendicant is someone who lives by begging, often a friar.

clue.text: Make laws support international reprimand

parts.note: a leg supports a table
i = international
to slate someone is to criticise them harshly

explanation.surface: Lawmakers backing an international reprimand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' reads as backing a motion; it is a leg, as of a table. Slate as a verb is British for to criticise severely.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: the word comes from Latin lex, legis, meaning law.

clue.text: Straggling, agent accepts rocky ride

indicators.note: The agent accepts the other letters inside himself.

parts.note: a spy is a secret agent

indicators.note: Something rocky is unsteady and shaken, so the letters are jumbled.

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Lagging behind, a secret agent puts up with a bumpy journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocky ride' reads as a rough time; 'rocky' is the instruction to shake up the letters of 'ride'.
explanation.definitionFit: Spidery handwriting is thin and straggling, sprawling like a spider's legs.

clue.text: Level compass

definitions.meaning: a verb here: to set things in an even line

explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like tools, a spirit level and a drawing compass; neither is meant as an object.
explanation.definitionFit: To range is to set in a line, to level; and compass, in its old sense of scope, is a range.

clue.text: Old angler in fantastic Dorset river

indicators.note: Something fantastic is fanciful, remade in a strange new form.

parts.note: anagram fodder
r = river

explanation.surface: A veteran fisherman on a splendid river in Dorset.
explanation.walkthrough: Dorset is a county in south-west England famous for chalk streams; 'Dorset river' sounds like one named stream, but the county's letters and the river's one letter are mixed together.
explanation.definitionFit: Rodster is an archaic word for an angler, one who fishes with a rod.

clue.text: Ornamental moulding base these days found in search engine

indicators.note: What is found in something sits inside it.

parts.note: Bing is Microsoft's search engine
e is the base of natural logarithms
AD, anno Domini, is the present era

explanation.surface: Looking up a decorative moulding online nowadays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' pulls towards the bottom of a moulding; it is the mathematical constant e.
explanation.definitionFit: Beading is a narrow decorative moulding shaped like a row of beads.

clue.text: Did something outstanding either side of tense day

indicators.note: Standing either side of something is to enclose it.

parts.note: ace = excellent
t = tense, in grammar
d = day

explanation.surface: Someone excelled on both sides of a tense day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Did something outstanding' looks like one definition; only 'Did something' defines, and 'outstanding' is the ace.
explanation.definitionFit: To act is to do something, so acted matches the past tense.

clue.text: Red mollusc eating earth cast up

indicators.note: In a down clue, cast up means thrown upward, reading bottom to top.
What is eaten goes inside the eater.

parts.note: a slug is a shell-less mollusc
e = earth, on electric plugs

explanation.surface: A red slug swallowing soil and bringing it back up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast up' sounds like vomiting, which fits the eating slug; in a down answer it means reading upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossword favourite from heraldry, where the colours keep Norman French names, and red on a coat of arms goes by this one.

clue.text: Revolutionary having petulant complaint overheard in tent?

parts.note: a Red is a communist revolutionary

indicators.note: What is overheard reaches us by ear, so the word is spelt another way.

parts.note: a whine is a peevish complaint

explanation.surface: A rebel whose sulky grumbling can be heard through the canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tent' is not canvas: it is a deep-red Spanish wine, and the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Tent, from Spanish tinto, is a dark red wine, so red wine is what is in a glass of tent.

clue.text: Garden tool left out of financial inventory

parts.note: a ledger is a book of accounts
l = left

explanation.surface: A garden tool missing from the accounts register.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left out of' reads as one idea; 'left' gives L and 'out of' removes it.
explanation.definitionFit: An edger is a tool for trimming the edges of a lawn.

clue.text: What was quick bite, lunch having been organised

indicators.note: Organised letters have been set out afresh in a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A snack eaten fast once lunch had been arranged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What was quick bite' reads as a fast snack; 'quick' is an old word for pregnant, as in 'quick with child'. In the club is British slang for pregnant.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Quick' formerly meant pregnant, with a child that had quickened, so what was once called quick is now in the club.

clue.text: Fly from the east, absorbing western accent

indicators.note: In an across answer, reading from the east means right to left.
Something absorbing takes another inside it.

parts.note: a gnat is a small fly
w = western

explanation.surface: A traveller flying in from the east picks up a Western accent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' looks like a verb of air travel; it is the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this is one particular nasal kind of accent, heard in some American and Australian speech.

clue.text: This time, sycophant puts forward Democrat

parts.note: a toady flatters for favour
D = Democrat

explanation.surface: On this occasion a flatterer promotes a Democrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puts forward' sounds like nominating a candidate; it moves the D one place towards the front of TOADY.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the present occasion, as in 'this time I mean it'.

clue.text: Correspondent occasionally having to work in The Cloud?

definitions.text: Correspondent occasionally having to work in The Cloud?

parts.note: reads as a part-time journalist or letter writer
the capitals suggest online storage, but the work is done up among real clouds

explanation.walkthrough: 'The Cloud' in capitals suggests online storage; it is the actual sky, where a skywriter's smoke letters appear.
explanation.definitionFit: A skywriter traces messages in smoke from a plane, writing in the clouds now and then.
